result.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): B is the better answer overall: it has a cleaner token set (four durations, three easings), says outright that the numbers are starting points to tune, and has a short, clear process for changing them, which makes it easy to use as documentation. A is more thorough, with a reduced-motion fallback for each pattern and an explicit list of what not to animate. But it uses literal values like 160ms, 120ms and 1000ms even though its own checklist bans literal values, it is too long for quick lookup, and it never says the numbers are meant to be tuned. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): A gives a tight, consistent token set (4 durations, 3 easings) and a clear recipe per pattern, so a developer can actually use it as documentation, along with a short process for proposing changes. B is more thorough and has an excellent per-preset reduced-motion column and a don't-animate list. However, it breaks its own 'no literal ms' rule (120ms, 160ms, 150ms, 1000ms in the table) and grows well past the request with loading, error, and live-data guidance. A's reduced-motion rule is global rather than spelled out per pattern, which is its main weakness.
